topics.name: Rhode Island
topics.kicker: Smallest state · Roger Williams’s colony of religious freedom
topics.briefing: Rhode Island is the smallest state, but its history is full of rebels. Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636 after Massachusetts banished him, and the colony became a haven for people of many faiths. Its colonists burned a British ship in the Gaspee Affair, and Samuel Slater built America’s first successful water-powered cotton-spinning mill there, but it was the last of the 13 original states to approve the Constitution.
topics.answerHtml: Rhode Island (accept Rhode Island and Providence Plantations; do not accept “Providence”)
accept: colony of rhode island and providence plantations
state of rhode island and providence plantations

tossups.p: A 1663 royal charter from King Charles II called this colony a “lively experiment” in full religious freedom, and that charter served as its constitution until 1843. John Clarke spent years in London winning that charter for this colony.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams, which became the smallest U.S. state.

tossups.p: This state and Connecticut were the only two states that never ratified the 18th Amendment, which created national Prohibition. The painter Gilbert Stuart, whose portrait of George Washington appears on the one-dollar bill, was born here in 1755.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, home to the cities of Providence and Newport.

tossups.p: George Washington promised “to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance” in a 1790 letter to the Jewish congregation in this state’s city of Newport. That congregation’s Touro Synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, founded as a colony by Roger Williams.

tossups.p: In 1772, merchant John Brown led a group of colonists who rowed out and burned the British customs schooner _Gaspee_ after it ran aground while chasing another ship in this colony’s waters. A royal commission later failed to find anyone willing to name the attackers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England colony, later the smallest state, whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Samuel Slater memorized the designs of British textile machines and then, with money from the Quaker merchant Moses Brown, built a water-powered cotton-spinning mill in this state’s village of Pawtucket [“puh-TUCK-it”]. People in Britain called him “Slater the Traitor.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England state where Slater helped start the American Industrial Revolution.

tossups.p: In the 1840s, Thomas Dorr led a rebellion because this state kept using its 1663 royal charter as its constitution, and only men who owned land could vote. Supporters of his “People’s Constitution” even elected Dorr governor, so this state briefly had two rival governments.
tossups.r: The rebellion led to a new state constitution in 1843. For 10 points, name this New England state whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Anne Hutchinson’s followers founded Portsmouth on Aquidneck [“uh-KWID-nek”] Island, the island this colony was named for, after Massachusetts banished her. William Coddington and John Clarke later founded Newport at the other end of that island.
tossups.r: Roger Williams had already founded Providence nearby. For 10 points, name this colony, which became the smallest state.

tossups.p: On May 4, 1776, two months before the Declaration of Independence, this colony’s legislature renounced its loyalty to King George III. Years later, it refused to send delegates to the Constitutional Convention and became the last of the thirteen original states to ratify the Constitution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, which finally ratified in 1790 and is the smallest of the fifty states.

tossups.p: Oliver Hazard Perry, the hero of the Battle of Lake Erie, and his younger brother Matthew, who opened Japan to American trade, were both born in this state. Earlier, Nathanael Greene of this state became one of George Washington’s most trusted generals.
tossups.r: Greene and Roger Williams represent it in the National Statuary Hall Collection. For 10 points, name this New England state whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: In 1778, this state’s 1st Regiment, which included many Black and Native American soldiers, held its ground against repeated attacks during a battle on Aquidneck Island. A French fleet had come to help the Americans in that campaign but sailed away before the battle.
tossups.r: That battle followed a failed attempt to retake Newport from the British. For 10 points, name this New England state, whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Gilded Age millionaires built enormous summer “cottages” in this state’s city of Newport, including The Breakers, built for Cornelius Vanderbilt II. Newport is also home to the Naval War College and the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
tossups.r: Its capital is Providence. For 10 points, name this smallest of the fifty states.

tossups.p: The Ivy League college in this state was renamed in 1804 for Nicholas Brown Jr., a merchant whose family had long supported it. That college, first founded in 1764, had moved to this state’s capital in 1770.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, home to Brown University and the capital city of Providence.

tossups.p: This state’s town of Bristol claims the oldest continuous Fourth of July celebration in the country, first held in 1785. Coffee milk was named its official state drink in 1993, and its flag shows a golden anchor above the one-word motto “Hope.”
tossups.r: Its capital is Providence. For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, nicknamed the Ocean State.

tossups.p: Jewish families settled in this colony’s town of Newport in the 1650s, and Quakers were allowed to worship freely there while other New England colonies punished them. Its founder had been banished from Massachusetts in 1635 for spreading “new and dangerous opinions.”
tossups.r: Critics called it “Rogues’ Island.” For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams.

tossups.p: Stephen Hopkins and William Ellery signed the Declaration of Independence for this colony, and Hopkins’s brother Esek became the first commander in chief of the Continental Navy. Stephen Hopkins had earlier served several terms as this colony’s governor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams, later the smallest state.

trap.title: Colony, city, or founder?
trap.body: Many Rhode Island tossups lean on Roger Williams and Providence, which have their own answer lines: Roger Williams is the man, and Providence is the capital city he founded in 1636. Neighbors cause trouble too: Massachusetts banished both Williams and Anne Hutchinson, and Thomas Hooker led his congregation from Massachusetts to found Hartford, Connecticut.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This colony” or “this state” with the Gaspee, Slater’s mill, Touro Synagogue, the Dorr Rebellion, or the last ratification of the Constitution means Rhode Island; “this man” means Roger Williams; “this city” means Providence or Newport. The old official name, “Rhode Island and Providence Plantations,” is also fine, but “Providence” alone names a city.
trap.line: Real answer line: Rhode Island (accept Rhode Island and Providence Plantations)

topics.name: Roe v. Wade
topics.kicker: 1973 Supreme Court abortion ruling · Overruled by Dobbs in 2022
topics.briefing: _Roe v. Wade_ is one of the most famous and most debated Supreme Court cases in U.S. history. In 1973, the Court ruled 7–2 for “Jane Roe,” a Texas woman whose real name was Norma McCorvey, holding that a constitutional right to privacy covers a woman’s decision whether to have an abortion. In 2022, the Court overruled Roe in _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_, returning the question of abortion laws to the states.
topics.answerHtml: Roe v. Wade (prompt on “Roe” or “Wade” alone; do not accept “abortion”)
reject: dobbs v jackson womens health organization

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Sarah Weddington, who was only 26 when she first argued this case before the Supreme Court, and Linda Coffee represented its plaintiff, a Texas woman named Norma McCorvey. To protect her privacy, the plaintiff was given a pseudonym in this case.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court decision that was overruled by _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_.

tossups.p: The defendant in this case was a Texas district attorney whose office had prosecuted Jack Ruby, the man who shot Lee Harvey Oswald. That district attorney served Dallas County for more than thirty years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case about abortion and the right to privacy.

tossups.p: This case was argued twice before the Supreme Court, in December 1971 and October 1972, because Lewis Powell and William Rehnquist [“REN-kwist”] joined the Court after the first argument. In the 7–2 decision, Rehnquist and Byron White dissented.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case about the right to privacy and abortion.

tossups.p: On the same day it decided this case, the Supreme Court also struck down parts of a Georgia law in a companion case, _Doe v. Bolton_, which was brought by a woman using the name “Mary Doe.” Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the majority opinions in both cases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision that struck down a Texas law restricting abortion.

tossups.p: The author of this decision’s majority opinion had worked as a lawyer for the Mayo Clinic before Richard Nixon appointed him to the Supreme Court. That justice, Harry Blackmun, based this decision on a right to privacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case that the Supreme Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: A 1992 joint opinion by Sandra Day O’Connor, Anthony Kennedy, and David Souter kept the core of this decision but replaced its trimester framework with an “undue burden” test. That case, _Planned Parenthood v. Casey_, involved a Pennsylvania law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision about abortion, written by Harry Blackmun.

tossups.p: In May 2022, the news site _Politico_ published a leaked draft of a Supreme Court opinion that would overrule this decision. The final opinion, written by Samuel Alito, upheld a Mississippi law and returned the question of abortion laws to the states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case that was overruled in _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_.

tossups.p: This decision built on _Griswold v. Connecticut_, a 1965 case in which Justice William O. Douglas wrote that guarantees in the Bill of Rights have “penumbras” that create zones of privacy. Douglas also joined the majority in this decision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case that struck down a Texas abortion law.

tossups.p: The plaintiff in this case later revealed her identity, and in 1995 she announced that she had changed her views and would work with groups that opposed this decision. That plaintiff, Norma McCorvey, had used a pseudonym when the case began in Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case decided by a 7–2 vote.

tossups.p: This decision created a framework that divided pregnancy into three trimesters and allowed states to regulate abortion more as a pregnancy went on. Nineteen years later, the Supreme Court dropped that framework but kept the core of this decision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case named for a Texas plaintiff and a Dallas district attorney.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Warren Burger and Thurgood Marshall were among the seven justices in the majority in this decision, which was announced on January 22, 1973. Its majority opinion traced the history of laws on its subject back to ancient times, including ancient Greece and Rome.
tossups.r: It said a right to privacy covers a woman’s decision whether to have an abortion. For 10 points, name this case that the Supreme Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: The case that overruled this decision was named for Thomas Dobbs, Mississippi’s top state health officer, and a clinic in the state’s capital. That 2022 ruling said that the Constitution does not grant a right to abortion and left the question to the states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision, written by Harry Blackmun, that the _Dobbs_ case overruled.

tossups.p: In 1970, a three-judge federal court in Dallas declared the law challenged in this case unconstitutional but did not order Texas to stop enforcing it. The Supreme Court then struck down that law, which banned abortion except to save the woman’s life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court decision, written by Harry Blackmun, about the right to privacy.

tossups.p: The lower court in this case found a right to privacy in the Ninth Amendment, but the Supreme Court’s majority said that right was founded in the Fourteenth Amendment’s concept of personal liberty. Harry Blackmun wrote that majority opinion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case about abortion that the Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: When the Supreme Court overruled this decision in 2022, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan wrote a joint dissent, while Chief Justice John Roberts voted to uphold the state law but would not have overruled this decision entirely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision that had recognized a constitutional right to abortion.

trap.title: Which abortion case?
trap.body: Three Supreme Court cases come up together. _Roe v. Wade_ (1973) recognized a constitutional right to abortion; _Planned Parenthood v. Casey_ (1992) kept that right but replaced Roe’s trimester framework with an “undue burden” test; and _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_ (2022) overruled both and returned the issue to the states. Answering only “abortion,” or naming the wrong case, will not get credit.
trap.fix: Listen for the year and the names: 1973, Harry Blackmun, “Jane Roe,” Henry Wade, Texas, and trimesters mean _Roe v. Wade_; 1992, Pennsylvania, and “undue burden” mean _Casey_; 2022, Mississippi, Samuel Alito, and the leaked draft mean _Dobbs_.
trap.line: Real answer line: Roe v. Wade (do not accept “abortion” alone)

topics.name: Ronald Reagan
topics.kicker: 40th U.S. President · Actor turned governor and Cold War leader
topics.briefing: Ronald Reagan was a radio sports announcer, a Hollywood actor, and president of the Screen Actors Guild before he became governor of California. As the 40th president, from 1981 to 1989, he cut income taxes, survived being shot just 69 days into his first term, and urged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down this wall” in Berlin. In 1987, the two leaders signed a treaty that eliminated a whole class of nuclear missiles.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This actor’s line “Where’s the rest of me?”, from the film _Kings Row_, became the title of his first autobiography. He also played the football player George Gipp in _Knute Rockne, All American_, which gave him a lasting nickname.
tossups.r: He later served as governor of California. For 10 points, name this actor who became the 40th president.

tossups.p: As a young radio announcer in Des Moines, Iowa, this man described Chicago Cubs games that he re-created from short telegraph reports. Earlier, he had worked as a lifeguard in Dixon, Illinois, and graduated from Eureka College.
tossups.r: He later became a Hollywood actor. For 10 points, name this man who was elected president in 1980.

tossups.p: This man’s televised 1964 speech “A Time for Choosing,” given in support of Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign, launched his own political career. He had switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party two years earlier.
tossups.r: Two years after that speech, he was elected governor of California. For 10 points, name this man who served as the 40th president from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: In 1947, this actor testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee while serving as president of the Screen Actors Guild. In the 1950s, he hosted _General Electric Theater_ on television and gave speeches at the company’s factories.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former actor and governor of California who became president in 1981.

tossups.p: After this president was shot, Secretary of State Alexander Haig told reporters, “I am in control here.” Press secretary James Brady was also wounded in that attack, and a 1993 law requiring background checks for handgun buyers was later named for Brady.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who survived being shot by John Hinckley Jr. in 1981.

tossups.p: In August 1981, this president fired more than 11,000 air traffic controllers after their union, PATCO, went on strike in violation of a law banning strikes by federal workers. That same month, he signed a large cut in income tax rates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president who had been a Hollywood actor and governor of California.

tossups.p: In a 1983 speech to a meeting of evangelical Christians, this president called the Soviet Union an “evil empire.” About two weeks later, he proposed a missile defense system that critics nicknamed “Star Wars.”
tossups.r: That plan was the Strategic Defense Initiative. For 10 points, name this 40th president, who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: This president’s 1986 summit with Mikhail Gorbachev [“GOR-buh-chawf”] in Reykjavík [“RAYK-yuh-vik”], Iceland, nearly produced a deal to get rid of nuclear weapons, but it broke down over his missile defense plan. A year later, the two leaders signed the INF Treaty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who, in Berlin, told Gorbachev to “tear down this wall.”

tossups.p: The Tower Commission investigated a scandal in which members of this president’s administration secretly sold weapons to Iran, hoping to free American hostages in Lebanon, and sent some of the profits to rebels fighting Nicaragua’s government, even though Congress had banned that aid. Marine officer Oliver North was a central figure in that affair.
tossups.r: Those rebels were called the Contras. For 10 points, name this president whose administration faced the Iran-Contra affair.

tossups.p: This president made William Rehnquist [“REN-kwist”] Chief Justice and appointed Antonin Scalia to the Supreme Court in 1986, but the Senate rejected his nominee Robert Bork the next year. Five years earlier, he had appointed the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court.
tossups.r: That woman was Sandra Day O’Connor. For 10 points, name this president who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: This president signed the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, which formally apologized to Japanese Americans who had been forced into camps during World War II. Two years earlier, he signed an immigration law that gave legal status to nearly three million people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 40th president, a former actor and governor of California.

tossups.p: After the space shuttle _Challenger_ broke apart in 1986, this president said its crew had “slipped the surly bonds of earth” to “touch the face of God,” words from the poem “High Flight.” That night, he spoke from the Oval Office instead of giving his State of the Union address.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president, a former actor and governor of California, who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: In a 1984 debate, this president promised not to exploit “my opponent’s youth and inexperience” for political purposes. That fall, he carried 49 states against Walter Mondale, after a campaign that included an ad declaring it was “morning again in America.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican, the oldest person elected president up to that time.

tossups.p: In his first inaugural address, this president said that “in this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.” Minutes after he took the oath of office, Iran released the 52 Americans it had held hostage for 444 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who had defeated Jimmy Carter in the 1980 election.

tossups.p: In a handwritten 1994 letter, this former president told Americans that he had Alzheimer’s disease. While in office, he had signed the 1983 law creating a national holiday honoring Martin Luther King Jr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who told Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down this wall” in 1987.

trap.title: Reagan or Bush?
trap.body: George H. W. Bush was Ronald Reagan’s vice president for all eight years and then became the 41st president, so 1980s Cold War clues can fit either man. The Berlin Wall actually fell in November 1989, during Bush’s first year, even though Reagan’s “Tear down this wall!” speech came in 1987. Iran clues are another trap: the hostage crisis belongs to Jimmy Carter, though the hostages were freed minutes after Reagan took office.
trap.fix: Reagan clues: acting, the Screen Actors Guild, governor of California, the 1981 assassination attempt, the air traffic controllers, “Reaganomics,” “evil empire,” SDI, Iran-Contra, and the INF Treaty. Bush clues: the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Persian Gulf War, and “Read my lips: no new taxes.” Terms named after him, like the Reagan Doctrine, are separate answers.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ronald Reagan (or Ronald Wilson Reagan)

topics.name: Rosa Parks
topics.kicker: Civil rights activist · Her 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
topics.briefing: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress and secretary of the local NAACP, refused a bus driver’s order to give up her seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, a 381-day protest led by a young Martin Luther King Jr. that ended after the courts struck down bus segregation. Congress later honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A few months before her most famous act, this woman attended a workshop on ending segregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee. She had served for years as secretary of her city’s NAACP chapter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, in December 1955 started a bus boycott.

tossups.p: In 1943, bus driver James F. Blake made this woman get off his bus so that she could re-enter through the back door, then drove away before she could get back on. She avoided riding his buses for years afterward.
tossups.r: In 1955, she refused Blake’s order to give up her seat. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest led to the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: E. D. Nixon, a leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, joined the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr to bail this woman out of jail. Nixon believed her case was the right one to challenge her city’s segregated buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this seamstress whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, sparked a famous bus boycott.

tossups.p: Nine months before this woman’s arrest, a 15-year-old named Claudette Colvin was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a bus in the same city. Colvin later became a plaintiff in _Browder v. Gayle_, the case that ended bus segregation there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus on December 1, 1955.

tossups.p: Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council stayed up all night printing leaflets after this woman’s arrest, calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on the day of her trial. That one-day protest grew into a boycott that lasted 381 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: The lawyer Fred Gray defended this woman after her arrest, then filed _Browder v. Gayle_ on behalf of four other women who had faced discrimination on city buses. In that case, a federal court ruled that bus segregation in this woman’s city was unconstitutional.
tossups.r: The Supreme Court upheld that ruling in 1956. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In 2013, this woman became the first Black woman honored with a full-length statue in the U.S. Capitol. When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honor in the Capitol Rotunda.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights activist who refused to give up her bus seat in 1955.

tossups.p: This woman worked in the Detroit office of Congressman John Conyers for more than twenty years, beginning in 1965. The Henry Ford Museum in nearby Dearborn displays the city bus from her most famous moment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose 1955 arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, led to a bus boycott.

tossups.p: This woman was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from her job as a seamstress at a department store when she made history. She later explained that she was not physically tired that evening: “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman, born with the last name McCauley in Tuskegee [“tuh-SKEE-gee”], Alabama, grew up on her grandparents’ farm in Pine Level. She married a barber named Raymond who was active in the NAACP.
tossups.r: She later became secretary of the NAACP’s Montgomery branch. For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus in 1955.

tossups.p: On December 5, 1955, this woman was found guilty of breaking her city’s bus segregation law and fined ten dollars plus court costs. That same day, a new group called the Montgomery Improvement Association chose a young minister as its leader.
tossups.r: That minister was Martin Luther King Jr. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman received the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996, and the Congressional Gold Medal in 1999. Congress also honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest on a Montgomery bus in 1955 sparked a year-long boycott.

tossups.p: This woman wrote a 1992 autobiography with Jim Haskins and a 1994 book about her faith called _Quiet Strength_. She moved to Detroit in 1957 after losing her job and receiving threats in Alabama.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: A well-known photograph of this woman being fingerprinted was actually taken in February 1956, when she and dozens of other boycott leaders were arrested under an old Alabama law against boycotts. Martin Luther King Jr. was also charged under that law.
tossups.r: Her first arrest had come months earlier on a city bus. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in December 1955 launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In November 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a ruling against segregated buses in this woman’s city, and the boycott there ended about a month later. During that boycott, many Black residents walked or shared rides in carpools instead of riding the buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), led by Martin Luther King Jr.
Honored by Congress as “the first lady of civil rights” and “the mother of the freedom movement”

Was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from work

trap.title: Woman, leader, or boycott?
trap.body: Several answer lines share this story. Claudette Colvin, a 15-year-old, refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus nine months before Rosa Parks did and later became a _Browder v. Gayle_ plaintiff. Martin Luther King Jr. led the boycott that Parks’s arrest started, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott itself is a separate answer, so listen for “this woman,” “this man,” or “this event.”
trap.fix: Parks clues: December 1, 1955, NAACP secretary, seamstress, the Highlander Folk School, James Blake, “tired of giving in,” and Detroit. Colvin clues: age 15, March 1955, and being a _Browder_ plaintiff. King clues: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, the Montgomery Improvement Association, and “I Have a Dream.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Rosa Parks (or Rosa Louise McCauley Parks)

topics.name: Battle of the Alamo
topics.kicker: Texian defenders fall in San Antonio, 1836 · A rallying cry for Texas
topics.briefing: For 13 days in 1836, about 200 Texian defenders held an old Spanish mission in San Antonio against the much larger Mexican army of General Antonio López de Santa Anna. Before dawn on March 6, the Mexican army stormed the walls, and nearly all the defenders died, including William Travis, Jim Bowie, and the frontier hero Davy Crockett. About six weeks later, Sam Houston’s soldiers shouted “Remember the Alamo!” as they defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto and won independence for Texas.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of the Alamo (or Siege of the Alamo; prompt on Texas Revolution or Mission San Antonio de Valero)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On February 24, 1836, a commander in this battle wrote a letter addressed “To the People of Texas & All Americans in the World,” vowing “I shall never surrender or retreat.” He signed that letter “Victory or Death” and sent it out with a messenger who slipped past the enemy army.
tossups.r: That commander was William Barret Travis. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle in San Antonio, where Jim Bowie and Davy Crockett died.

tossups.p: On March 1, 1836, thirty-two men from the town of Gonzales slipped through enemy lines to join the defenders in this battle, the only help that ever arrived. The next day, while this battle’s siege went on, delegates at Washington-on-the-Brazos adopted the Texas Declaration of Independence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 13-day siege that ended on March 6, 1836, with the deaths of nearly all of its Texian defenders.

tossups.p: The Tejano captain Juan Seguín [“seh-GEEN”] rode out of this battle’s fort as a messenger to seek help, so he survived to fight at San Jacinto weeks later. Help from James Fannin’s soldiers at Goliad [“GOH-lee-ad”] never arrived.
tossups.r: Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie were among this battle’s defenders. For 10 points, name this 1836 siege of a former Spanish mission in San Antonio, Texas.

tossups.p: After this battle, the winning general sent Susanna Dickinson, who had survived it with her baby daughter, Angelina, to carry news of the defeat to the Texian army at Gonzales. Joe, an enslaved man owned by one of this battle’s commanders, also survived.
tossups.r: Weeks later, Texans shouted this battle’s name as they attacked at San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this battle that ended on March 6, 1836.

tossups.p: According to a story first published decades later, a commander in this battle drew a line on the ground with his sword and asked every man willing to stay and fight to cross it. In that story, only Louis “Moses” Rose refused, and he escaped.
tossups.r: That commander was William Travis. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle in which Santa Anna’s army overran a fort in San Antonio.

tossups.p: When this battle’s siege began, the attacking army flew a red flag from a church tower, and during the final assault, its buglers played the “Degüello” [“day-GWAY-yoh”]. Both were signals that the defenders would be shown no mercy. Soldiers carrying ladders rushed the walls in the dark before dawn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that ended on March 6, 1836, when General Antonio López de Santa Anna’s Mexican army overwhelmed the Texian defenders of a San Antonio fort.

tossups.p: This battle was fought at a former Spanish mission called San Antonio de Valero, whose church later got its famous curved top from the U.S. Army in 1850. In December 1835, Texians had captured that mission and the town around it from General Martín Perfecto de Cos [“KOHSS”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of 1836, a Texian defeat that Sam Houston’s army avenged weeks later at San Jacinto.

tossups.p: Sam Houston suggested removing the cannons from this battle’s fort and abandoning it, but the officers there, including James Neill, decided to defend it instead. When Neill left on leave in February 1836, two men agreed to share command: a 26-year-old lawyer and a frontiersman famous for a large knife.
tossups.r: Those men were William Travis and Jim Bowie. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where they died alongside Davy Crockett.

tossups.p: In the early 1900s, Clara Driscoll used her own money to help save part of this battle’s site from being torn down, earning fame as its “Savior.” The Daughters of the Republic of Texas then managed that site for more than a hundred years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this San Antonio landmark and 1836 battle where William Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett died.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle, who called himself the “Napoleon of the West,” reached San Antonio on February 23 after marching his army north across the Rio Grande in winter. The outnumbered Texians in town rushed into an old mission when his troops appeared.
tossups.r: That general, Santa Anna, later lost at San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where Davy Crockett died.

tossups.p: John Wayne directed and starred in a 1960 film about this battle, playing a frontiersman who had once represented Tennessee in Congress. Fess Parker played that same frontiersman in a 1955 Disney movie that ends with this battle.
tossups.r: That frontiersman was Davy Crockett. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle in which Santa Anna’s army defeated Texian defenders in San Antonio.

tossups.p: In 2014, the English rock musician Phil Collins gave the State of Texas his huge collection of objects related to this battle. In 2015, this battle’s site became part of a World Heritage Site that includes five Spanish missions in San Antonio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that ended on March 6, 1836, when Santa Anna’s army defeated a small Texian force.

tossups.p: A former congressman reached this battle’s fort in February 1836 with a small group of volunteers from Tennessee, months after he lost his race for reelection. Years earlier, he had broken with Andrew Jackson by voting against the Indian Removal Act.
tossups.r: That man was Davy Crockett. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle in San Antonio, Texas, where Crockett died.

tossups.p: The war that included this battle began in October 1835 at Gonzales, where Texians refused to hand over a small cannon and flew a flag reading “Come and Take It.” Tejano defenders in this battle included Gregorio Esparza, whose young son Enrique survived and later told its story.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in San Antonio whose name became a battle cry when Texas won its independence at San Jacinto.

tossups.p: One commander in this battle gave his name to a large hunting knife, but he became so sick during the siege that he could not get out of bed. Years earlier, he had married into a leading Tejano family of San Antonio.
tossups.r: That man, Jim Bowie, died in this battle along with Davy Crockett. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle in San Antonio, Texas.

General Antonio López de Santa Anna’s much larger Mexican army defeated the Texian defenders
Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie died defending the fort
Its name became a battle cry (“Remember the …!”) when Sam Houston’s army beat Santa Anna at San Jacinto on April 21, 1836

Legend: Travis drew a line in the sand with his sword and asked those who would stay to cross it; only Moses Rose refused
Survivors: Susanna Dickinson and her baby Angelina, sent by Santa Anna to warn the Texian army at Gonzales, and Joe, Travis’s enslaved servant
Texas declared independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos on March 2, 1836, during the siege
The only reinforcements: 32 men from Gonzales, who slipped in on March 1
Jim Bowie, namesake of the Bowie knife, had married into a leading Tejano family; he was too sick to leave his bed
Tejanos: captain Juan Seguín left as a messenger and later fought at San Jacinto; defender Gregorio Esparza’s young son Enrique survived

Travis, a 26-year-old lawyer, shared command with Bowie after Neill left on leave

The U.S. Army gave the old mission church its famous curved top in 1850
Clara Driscoll (its “Savior”) helped save the site; the Daughters of the Republic of Texas managed it for over 100 years

John Wayne directed a 1960 film about it and played Crockett; Fess Parker played Crockett in a 1955 Disney movie
Phil Collins donated his collection of its artifacts (2014); part of the San Antonio Missions World Heritage Site (2015)

trap.title: Alamo or San Jacinto?
trap.body: The Texas Revolution had two famous battles in 1836. The Alamo (February 23–March 6, San Antonio) was a Texian defeat; San Jacinto (April 21) was the Texian victory in which Sam Houston’s army shouted “Remember the Alamo!” and captured Santa Anna. Davy Crockett and Santa Anna are separate answer lines, so naming the man instead of the battle is wrong.
trap.fix: Travis, Bowie, Crockett, a 13-day siege, the Gonzales 32, and “Victory or Death” mean the Alamo. Sam Houston’s surprise attack, a battle of about 18 minutes, and Santa Anna’s capture mean San Jacinto. Hearing “Remember the Alamo!” as a battle cry usually means the question is about San Jacinto.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of the Alamo (or Siege of the Alamo; prompt on Texas Revolution or Mission San Antonio de Valero)

topics.name: Vice President of the United States
topics.kicker: Second-highest office in the U.S. government · First in line for the presidency
topics.briefing: The vice president has two jobs written into the Constitution: presiding over the Senate, where the vice president votes only to break a tie, and standing ready to take over the presidency. Nine vice presidents have become president in the middle of a term, starting with John Tyler in 1841. John Adams, the first vice president, called it “the most insignificant office” ever invented, while Kamala Harris, the first woman to hold it (2021–2025), cast a record number of tie-breaking votes.
topics.answerHtml: Vice President of the United States (accept VP or vice presidency; prompt on President of the Senate; do not accept “President”)
accept: vice president of the united states
the vice president of the united states
vice president of the united states of america
the vice president of the united states of america
reject: speaker of the house of representatives
president pro tempore of the senate

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The first person to hold this office complained in a letter to his wife that his country had given him “the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived or his imagination conceived.”
tossups.r: That man, John Adams, held this office under George Washington. For 10 points, name this office whose holder is first in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Before 1804, this office went to whoever finished second in the Electoral College, which is how Thomas Jefferson came to serve in it under his rival John Adams. After the election of 1800 ended in a tie, the Twelfth Amendment had electors vote for this office separately.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate and takes over if the president dies.

tossups.p: In 1837, the Senate chose Richard Mentor Johnson for this office, the only time it has done so, after no candidate won a majority of electoral votes. Johnson served in this office under Martin Van Buren, who had held it under Andrew Jackson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office whose holder casts tie-breaking votes in the Senate and is first in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Critics called one holder of this office “His Accidency” after he claimed the full title and powers of the presidency in 1841, instead of acting as a temporary caretaker. He took over when William Henry Harrison died just a month into his term.
tossups.r: That man was John Tyler. For 10 points, name this office, whose holder becomes president when a president dies.

tossups.p: Section 2 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment, ratified in 1967, lets the president fill a vacancy in this office if both houses of Congress approve. Nelson Rockefeller became the second person chosen that way, in 1974.
tossups.r: The first was Gerald Ford, who replaced Spiro Agnew in 1973. For 10 points, name this office, second in rank only to the presidency.

tossups.p: John C. Calhoun became the first person to resign from this office when he left it in 1832 to take a seat in the Senate. He and George Clinton are the only people to hold this office under two different presidents.
tossups.r: Calhoun’s record of 31 tie-breaking votes in this office lasted until Kamala Harris broke it in 2023. For 10 points, name this office.

tossups.p: Since the late 1970s, holders of this office have lived at Number One Observatory Circle, a house on the grounds of the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C. Congress made that house the official home for this office in 1974, and Walter Mondale was the first to live there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, first in the presidential line of succession, ahead of the Speaker of the House.

tossups.p: Charles Curtis, a member of the Kaw Nation, became the first person of Native American ancestry to hold this office when Herbert Hoover took office in 1929. Elbridge Gerry, the namesake of gerrymandering, died while holding this office in 1814.
tossups.r: Kamala Harris became the first woman to hold it in 2021. For 10 points, name this office.

tossups.p: Alben Barkley’s grandson came up with the nickname “the Veep” for him while he held this office under Harry Truman. Truman himself had held this office for only 82 days before Franklin Roosevelt died in 1945.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office whose holder takes over if a president dies, resigns, or is removed.

tossups.p: In 1988, George H. W. Bush became the first person since Martin Van Buren in 1836 to be elected president while holding this office. Before Van Buren, only John Adams and Thomas Jefferson had done so.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office whose holder casts tie-breaking votes as President of the Senate.

tossups.p: While holding this office, Thomas Jefferson wrote a manual of parliamentary practice for the Senate. The House of Representatives later made parts of that manual part of its own rules.
tossups.r: Article I says this office’s holder “shall have no Vote, unless they be equally divided.” For 10 points, name this office.

tossups.p: In 1923, Calvin Coolidge was sworn in as president by his own father, a notary public, by the light of a kerosene lamp at the family farmhouse in Vermont. Coolidge had been in this office when Warren Harding died.
tossups.r: Nine holders of this office have become president in the middle of a term. For 10 points, name this office.

tossups.p: Franklin Roosevelt had three different holders of this office: John Nance Garner, Henry Wallace, and Harry Truman. Truman was never told about the secret atomic bomb project while he held this office, and he learned of it only after becoming president.
tossups.r: Truman became president when Roosevelt died in 1945. For 10 points, name this office.

tossups.p: Under Section 4 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment, the holder of this office and a majority of the Cabinet can declare that the president is unable to serve. Under Section 3 of that amendment, Dick Cheney briefly became acting president twice while George W. Bush had medical procedures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder becomes president if the president dies, resigns, or is removed.

tossups.p: While holding this office, Aaron Burr killed Alexander Hamilton in an 1804 duel, and a few months later he presided over the Senate impeachment trial of Supreme Court justice Samuel Chase, who was acquitted.
tossups.r: Burr held this office under Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this office, which John Adams held first.

John Adams called it “the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived”

George H. W. Bush (1988) was the first sitting holder elected president since Martin Van Buren (1836)
Thomas Jefferson wrote a manual of parliamentary practice for the Senate while holding it; the House later adopted parts of it
Calvin Coolidge was sworn in by his father, a notary public, by kerosene lamp in Vermont (1923)
25th Amendment, Section 4: it and most of the Cabinet can declare a president unable to serve; under Section 3, Dick Cheney was briefly acting president
Elbridge Gerry, namesake of gerrymandering, died in office (1814)
Franklin Roosevelt had three: John Nance Garner, Henry Wallace, and Harry Truman
Burr presided over the Senate impeachment trial of Justice Samuel Chase, who was acquitted (1805)

trap.title: Office, not officeholder
trap.body: Questions about this office are full of famous people who held it, such as John Adams, John Tyler, Gerald Ford, and Kamala Harris, so it is tempting to buzz with a name. Players also mix it up with the next people in the line of succession: the Speaker of the House is second, the President pro tempore of the Senate is third, and the Secretary of State is fourth. Saying just “President” is wrong.
trap.fix: If the question says “this office” or “this position,” answer “vice president.” Presiding over the Senate and breaking ties means the vice president; leading the House means the Speaker; the President pro tempore runs the Senate when the vice president is away.
trap.line: Real answer line: Vice President of the United States (accept VP or vice presidency; prompt on President of the Senate; do not accept “President”)

topics.name: Wounded Knee massacre
topics.kicker: Soldiers kill hundreds of Lakota, 1890 · Often called the end of the Indian Wars
topics.briefing: On December 29, 1890, soldiers of the U.S. 7th Cavalry surrounded a band of Lakota people led by Spotted Elk (also called Big Foot) at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota. As the soldiers were taking away the Lakota’s weapons, a shot rang out and the soldiers opened fire, killing hundreds of men, women, and children. The massacre followed government fears of the Ghost Dance and the killing of Sitting Bull two weeks earlier.
topics.answerHtml: Wounded Knee Massacre (accept Battle of Wounded Knee; prompt on Ghost Dance War or Pine Ridge Campaign)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Oglala holy man Black Elk later said that “a people’s dream died there” when he remembered this event in the book _Black Elk Speaks_, which he told to the poet John Neihardt. Black Elk had ridden to the scene as a young man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre of hundreds of Lakota people by U.S. soldiers in South Dakota.

tossups.p: Dee Brown took the title of his 1970 history of the American West, told from Native Americans’ point of view, from a poem by Stephen Vincent Benét [“beh-NAY”] called “American Names,” which mentions the place where this event happened. That book ends with this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this massacre at a creek on South Dakota’s Pine Ridge Reservation on December 29, 1890.

tossups.p: After a vision during a solar eclipse, the Paiute prophet Wovoka [“woh-VOH-kuh”] taught that a sacred dance could bring back the buffalo and reunite the living with their ancestors. Lakota followers of his movement wore special shirts that they believed could stop bullets.
tossups.r: Fear of that movement, the Ghost Dance, helped lead to this event. For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre of Lakota people in South Dakota.

tossups.p: Kicking Bear and Short Bull traveled to Nevada to meet a prophet and brought his teachings home to the Lakota, which alarmed government agents on the reservations. Those agents called in the Army, setting off the events that led to this massacre.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1890 massacre at a creek on the Pine Ridge Reservation.

tossups.p: Some Hunkpapa [“HUNK-pah-pah”] people fled to join Spotted Elk’s band after Indian agency police killed their leader while trying to arrest him at Standing Rock, two weeks before this event. Spotted Elk’s band then set out for the Pine Ridge Agency.
tossups.r: That leader was Sitting Bull. For 10 points, name this December 1890 massacre of Lakota people by the 7th Cavalry.

tossups.p: The Miniconjou [“min-ee-KON-joo”] chief Spotted Elk, also called Big Foot, was sick with pneumonia when soldiers stopped his band and led it to the camp where this event happened. His band had been traveling to Pine Ridge after Red Cloud and other Oglala leaders invited him to help make peace.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this massacre of December 29, 1890, in which U.S. soldiers killed hundreds of Lakota.

tossups.p: Major Samuel Whitside’s troops stopped a Lakota band, and Colonel James Forsyth later ordered the Lakota to give up their weapons. A struggle over the rifle of a deaf man named Black Coyote came just before the shooting started in this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre of Lakota people carried out by the 7th Cavalry in South Dakota.

tossups.p: General Nelson Miles removed Colonel James Forsyth from command after this event and ordered an inquiry, but the War Department soon restored Forsyth to his post. Many of the people killed in this event were women and children.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1890 massacre of Lakota people at a South Dakota creek.

tossups.p: In 1973, Russell Means and Dennis Banks led a 71-day standoff with federal agents at the South Dakota town where this event had happened 83 years earlier. The protesters seized the town to protest broken treaties and the tribal chairman, Richard Wilson.
tossups.r: Those protesters belonged to the American Indian Movement. For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre of Lakota people by the 7th Cavalry.

tossups.p: In March 1973, Marlon Brando refused an Academy Award and sent Sacheen Littlefeather to speak about Hollywood’s treatment of Native Americans, while protesters were occupying the place where this event had happened.
tossups.r: That 71-day occupation was led by the American Indian Movement. For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre in South Dakota.

tossups.p: This event happened in the same year as the census that led officials to declare that the United States no longer had a frontier line. It took place on the Pine Ridge Reservation, home of the Oglala Lakota.
tossups.r: It is often called the end of the Indian Wars. For 10 points, name this massacre of Lakota people by the 7th Cavalry.

tossups.p: The ethnologist James Mooney visited Wovoka and wrote a long report on the religious movement that came before this massacre. The soldiers in this event belonged to the same regiment that George Armstrong Custer had led to defeat at the Little Bighorn 14 years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this massacre of Lakota people by the 7th Cavalry at a creek in South Dakota in December 1890.

tossups.p: Lakota riders on horseback have made December memorial rides that follow the route of Spotted Elk’s band to the place where this event happened, arriving on its anniversary. In 1990, a century after this event, Congress passed a resolution expressing “deep regret” for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this massacre of hundreds of Lakota people at a South Dakota creek on December 29, 1890.

tossups.p: An 1889 law broke the Great Sioux Reservation into smaller reservations, and cuts to food rations added to the hunger and anger that came before this event. Many Lakota then turned to a new religious movement for hope.
tossups.r: That movement, the Ghost Dance, spread before this event. For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre in South Dakota.

tossups.p: The Dakota doctor Charles Eastman treated survivors of this event, many of whom were brought to a church at the Pine Ridge Agency that was still decorated for Christmas. This event happened four days after Christmas, two weeks after Sitting Bull was killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1890 massacre of Lakota people by the 7th Cavalry in South Dakota.

clues.t: Happened at a creek in South Dakota on December 29, 1890
Soldiers of the U.S. 7th Cavalry killed hundreds of Lakota people, many of them women and children
Followed government fears of the Ghost Dance, a religious movement
Often called the end of the Indian Wars on the Great Plains
Took place on the Pine Ridge Reservation, home of the Oglala Lakota
The victims were the Miniconjou band of Spotted Elk (Big Foot), who was sick with pneumonia
Two weeks earlier (December 15, 1890), Indian agency police killed Sitting Bull while trying to arrest him at Standing Rock
The Ghost Dance began with the Paiute prophet Wovoka (Jack Wilson) of Nevada, after a vision during a solar eclipse
Lakota dancers wore “ghost shirts” that they believed could stop bullets
Soldiers were taking away the Lakota’s weapons when a shot rang out and the soldiers opened fire
1973: the American Indian Movement (AIM) occupied the town where it happened for 71 days
The 7th Cavalry was Custer’s old regiment, defeated at the Little Bighorn in 1876
Dee Brown’s 1970 book _Bury My Heart at …_ tells the story of the West from Native Americans’ point of view
Oglala holy man Black Elk: “a people’s dream died there” (_Black Elk Speaks_, told to John Neihardt)
Dee Brown’s title comes from Stephen Vincent Benét’s poem “American Names”
Kicking Bear and Short Bull visited Wovoka and brought the dance to the Lakota; alarmed agents called in the Army
Spotted Elk’s band was heading to Pine Ridge after Red Cloud and other Oglala leaders invited him to help make peace
Major Samuel Whitside stopped the band; Colonel James Forsyth commanded on December 29
A struggle over the rifle of a deaf man, Black Coyote, came just before the shooting
General Nelson Miles removed Forsyth from command, but the War Department restored him
Russell Means and Dennis Banks led the 1973 standoff with federal agents
Marlon Brando refused his Oscar during the 1973 occupation; Sacheen Littlefeather spoke for him
In 1990, a century later, Congress expressed “deep regret”; Lakota riders have retraced the band’s route in December memorial rides
An 1889 law split the Great Sioux Reservation into smaller reservations; cuts to food rations followed
Ethnologist James Mooney visited Wovoka and wrote a long report on the Ghost Dance
Came in the same year as the census that led officials to declare there was no longer a frontier line
Dakota doctor Charles Eastman treated survivors, many brought to a Pine Ridge church still decorated for Christmas

trap.title: Which massacre? Which battle?
trap.body: Several answer lines orbit this event. The Ghost Dance was the religious movement that alarmed officials, and Sitting Bull was killed two weeks earlier. The Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876) was the 7th Cavalry’s famous defeat under Custer, and the Sand Creek Massacre (1864) was a different attack, on Cheyenne and Arapaho people in Colorado.
trap.fix: December 1890, Spotted Elk (Big Foot), Pine Ridge, and the 1973 American Indian Movement standoff mean Wounded Knee. Custer’s Last Stand and 1876 mean the Little Bighorn; Colorado, John Chivington, and 1864 mean Sand Creek. If the question asks for “this religious movement,” say the Ghost Dance.
trap.line: Real answer line: Wounded Knee Massacre (accept Battle of Wounded Knee; prompt on Ghost Dance War or Pine Ridge Campaign)

topics.name: Al Capone
topics.kicker: Chicago gang boss of the Prohibition era · Jailed for tax evasion in 1931
topics.briefing: Al Capone led a Chicago gang that made millions of dollars selling illegal alcohol during Prohibition, and he was linked to many violent crimes. Prohibition agents, including Eliot Ness and his “Untouchables,” raided his breweries, but tax investigators finally brought him down: in 1931 he was convicted of income tax evasion and sentenced to 11 years in prison. He served part of that sentence at Alcatraz, left prison in poor health, and died in 1947.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1986, Geraldo Rivera hosted a live TV special in which workers broke into a secret vault beneath this man’s old headquarters at Chicago’s Lexington Hotel, but they found only dirt and a few empty bottles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Prohibition-era Chicago gang boss who was convicted of tax evasion in 1931.

tossups.p: In 1927, the Supreme Court ruled in _United States v. Sullivan_ that money earned from illegal businesses could be taxed, a decision that later let prosecutors go after this man, who had not filed tax returns for years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chicago gangster who was sent to prison for income tax evasion in 1931.

tossups.p: Treasury agent Frank Wilson found an old ledger that tied this man to the profits of a gambling house, helping to prove how much income he had never reported. Wilson worked for Elmer Irey’s special intelligence unit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gangster nicknamed “Scarface,” who was convicted of tax evasion in 1931.

tossups.p: On the first day of this man’s trial, Judge James Wilkerson swapped the entire jury with the jury from another trial, after reports that this man’s gang was trying to bribe or threaten jurors.
tossups.r: Wilkerson sentenced him to 11 years in prison. For 10 points, name this Chicago gang boss convicted of income tax evasion in 1931.

tossups.p: This man’s older brother Ralph, nicknamed “Bottles,” was convicted of tax evasion in 1930, a year before this man was convicted of the same crime. This man’s gang had moved its headquarters to Cicero, just outside Chicago, in the 1920s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gangster who made a fortune selling illegal alcohol during Prohibition.

tossups.p: In 1930, Frank Loesch’s Chicago Crime Commission named this man “Public Enemy Number One” on its list of gangsters. Five years earlier, he had taken over Johnny Torrio’s criminal organization when Torrio retired.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chicago gang boss of the Prohibition era who was later sent to Alcatraz.

tossups.p: This man’s business card claimed he was a “Second Hand Furniture Dealer,” and during the Great Depression he paid for a Chicago soup kitchen to improve his public image. That soup kitchen handed out free meals to thousands of jobless people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Prohibition-era gangster who was pursued by Eliot Ness and the “Untouchables.”

tossups.p: While working as a bouncer at a Coney Island club owned by Frankie Yale, this man was left with scars on his face after a fight, giving him a nickname he hated. He had been born in Brooklyn in 1899 to Italian immigrant parents.
tossups.r: That nickname was “Scarface.” For 10 points, name this gangster who led a Chicago gang during Prohibition.

tossups.p: While in federal prison, this man played the banjo in a band of inmates, and he was released in 1939 in poor health. He died in 1947 at his estate in Miami Beach, Florida.
tossups.r: He had served part of his sentence at Alcatraz. For 10 points, name this Chicago gangster convicted of tax evasion in 1931.

tossups.p: A Prohibition agent led a small squad that raided this man’s breweries and got its nickname because its members refused to take bribes. That agent’s memoir about this man’s downfall became a TV series starring Robert Stack.
tossups.r: That agent was Eliot Ness, leader of the Untouchables. For 10 points, name this Chicago gangster whom Ness pursued.

tossups.p: Robert De Niro played this man in a 1987 film directed by Brian De Palma, in which Sean Connery won an Oscar for playing a tough Chicago police officer who helps take this man down.
tossups.r: Kevin Costner played Eliot Ness in that film, _The Untouchables_. For 10 points, name this Prohibition-era Chicago gangster.

tossups.p: Paul Muni played a gangster loosely based on this man in Howard Hawks’s 1932 film _Scarface_, whose title echoed this man’s own hated nickname. This man’s real-life gang became known as the Chicago Outfit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gangster who got rich bootlegging during Prohibition and went to prison for tax evasion.

tossups.p: U.S. Attorney George E. Q. Johnson prosecuted this man, who at first agreed to plead guilty in exchange for a short sentence but withdrew his plea when the judge said he would not be bound by the deal.
tossups.r: This man was also linked to the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre. For 10 points, name this Chicago gangster convicted of tax evasion.

tossups.p: In August 1934, this man was moved from the federal prison in Atlanta to a new maximum-security prison on an island in San Francisco Bay, where he became one of its earliest and most famous inmates.
tossups.r: He had been sentenced to 11 years for tax evasion. For 10 points, name this Chicago gang boss of the Prohibition era.

tossups.p: In May 1929, this man was arrested in Philadelphia for carrying a concealed gun and spent several months in Eastern State Penitentiary, where a re-creation of his furnished cell is shown to visitors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chicago gangster whose biggest conviction came two years later, in 1931, for income tax evasion.

Made millions bootlegging (selling illegal alcohol) to speakeasies
Convicted of income tax evasion in 1931 and sentenced to 11 years
Nicknamed “Scarface” for scars on his face, a name he hated
Pursued by Eliot Ness and the “Untouchables,” Prohibition agents who refused bribes

Linked to the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre
