trap.title: Gangster, not G-man
trap.body: Capone questions are packed with names that are answer lines of their own: Eliot Ness (the agent who chased him), Johnny Torrio (the boss who brought him to Chicago), and John Dillinger (a 1930s bank robber who was also called “Public Enemy Number One”). Capone’s big conviction was not for bootlegging or violence but for income tax evasion, which surprises many players.
trap.fix: The agent who led the Untouchables is Ness; the gang boss they chased is Capone. If you hear “tax evasion,” “Alcatraz,” “Scarface,” or the Lexington Hotel, say Capone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Al Capone (or Alphonse Gabriel Capone; prompt on Scarface)

topics.name: American Revolutionary War
topics.kicker: Thirteen colonies vs. Great Britain, 1775–1783 · Won U.S. independence
topics.briefing: In April 1775, colonial militiamen traded shots with British soldiers at Lexington and Concord, and the thirteen colonies were soon at war with Great Britain, one of the world’s strongest powers. George Washington’s Continental Army lost many battles and survived a hungry winter at Valley Forge, but the Americans won a key victory at Saratoga and, with help from France, trapped a British army at Yorktown. In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, Britain recognized the United States as an independent nation.
topics.answerHtml: American Revolutionary War (or Revolutionary War; accept American War of Independence; prompt on Revolution or War of Independence)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Deborah Sampson disguised herself as a man named Robert Shurtleff to fight as a soldier in this war, and the legend of “Molly Pitcher,” who carried water to soldiers at the Battle of Monmouth in this war, may have been inspired by Mary Ludwig Hays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that began at Lexington and Concord in 1775 and won the United States its independence.

tossups.p: In 1775, Virginia’s royal governor, Lord Dunmore, promised freedom to enslaved people owned by Patriots if they escaped and joined the British army in this war. Thousands of Black Loyalists left with the British when this war ended, and many of them settled in Nova Scotia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war between Great Britain and its thirteen American colonies, which ended in 1783.

tossups.p: Bernardo de Gálvez [“GAHL-vess”], the Spanish governor of Louisiana, captured Pensacola from the British in 1781 during this war, after earlier taking Baton Rouge and Mobile. Spain had joined this war in 1779 as an ally of France.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which George Washington led the Continental Army against Great Britain.

tossups.p: King George III refused to receive the Olive Branch Petition, a last attempt at peace that John Dickinson wrote during the first months of this war, and instead declared that the colonies were in open rebellion.
tossups.r: That same year, the Second Continental Congress made George Washington commander of its army. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1775 to 1783.

tossups.p: During a 1779 sea battle in this war, John Paul Jones supposedly answered a demand to surrender by shouting, “I have not yet begun to fight!” His ship, the _Bonhomme Richard_, later sank, but he captured the British warship _Serapis_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which the young Continental Navy fought Great Britain from 1775 to 1783.

tossups.p: Francis Marion, nicknamed the “Swamp Fox,” led raids on British troops in South Carolina during this war, often striking from hiding places in the swamps. Daniel Morgan defeated Banastre Tarleton [“TAR-ul-tun”] at the Battle of Cowpens in this war.
tossups.r: Nathanael Greene commanded American forces in the South during this war. For 10 points, name this war that won American independence.

tossups.p: In 1780, Major John André [“AHN-dray”] was captured carrying plans showing how an American general meant to hand over the fort at West Point to the British in this war. André was executed as a spy.
tossups.r: That general was Benedict Arnold. For 10 points, name this war in which Arnold became a traitor.

tossups.p: Casimir Pulaski [“puh-LASS-kee”], called the “father of the American cavalry,” died after being wounded at the Siege of Savannah in this war, and the Polish engineer Thaddeus Kościuszko [“kosh-CHOOSH-koh”] designed fortifications at West Point.
tossups.r: The Marquis de Lafayette was a French volunteer in this war. For 10 points, name this war, fought from 1775 to 1783.

tossups.p: In the winter of this war’s first year, Henry Knox hauled cannons on sleds from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston. The British, who had won a costly victory at Bunker Hill months earlier, left the city in March 1776 after those guns appeared on Dorchester Heights.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that had begun at Lexington and Concord, in which George Washington led the Continental Army.

tossups.p: Thomas Paine opened the first essay in his series _The American Crisis_ with the words “These are the times that try men’s souls,” written during a dark moment of this war. Earlier, his pamphlet _Common Sense_ had urged Americans to break away from Britain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which George Washington crossed the Delaware to win at Trenton.

tossups.p: George Rogers Clark led a winter march through flooded country to capture Fort Sackville at Vincennes [“vin-SENZ”] in 1779, during this war, strengthening American claims to the land northwest of the Ohio River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1783, when Great Britain recognized the independence of the United States.

tossups.p: The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant led warriors on the British side in this war, while the Oneida [“oh-NY-duh”] Nation mostly fought for the Americans, splitting the Iroquois Confederacy. Raids on New York’s frontier led George Washington to send the Sullivan Expedition against the Iroquois in 1779.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Washington’s Continental Army fought Great Britain from 1775 to 1783.

tossups.p: John Burgoyne’s plan to cut off New England by marching south from Canada failed in this war when Horatio Gates’s army stopped him, and he surrendered his entire army in New York in October 1777.
tossups.r: That American victory at Saratoga brought France into this war as an ally. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1775 to 1783.

tossups.p: Baron von Steuben [“STOO-ben”] drilled soldiers during a hard winter in this war, and they used his training at the Battle of Monmouth, after which General Charles Lee was court-martialed for ordering a retreat.
tossups.r: That winter camp was at Valley Forge. For 10 points, name this war in which George Washington commanded the Continental Army.

tossups.p: Henry Laurens, who had been held in the Tower of London after the British captured him at sea, joined the American team that negotiated the treaty ending this war. That treaty set the western border of the new nation at the Mississippi River.
tossups.r: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay also negotiated that 1783 Treaty of Paris. For 10 points, name this war.

clues.t: Fought 1775–1783 between Great Britain and its thirteen American colonies, which won their independence
George Washington commanded the Continental Army
Began with the Battles of Lexington and Concord (April 19, 1775), “the shot heard round the world”
Lord Cornwallis’s surrender at Yorktown (1781) effectively ended the fighting
Ended by the Treaty of Paris (1783), negotiated by Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay
The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) came about a year into the fighting
Turning point: John Burgoyne surrendered to Horatio Gates at Saratoga (1777), and France joined the war in 1778
Bunker Hill (June 1775) was a costly British victory near Boston
Washington crossed the icy Delaware River and surprised the Hessians at Trenton (December 26, 1776)
Winter camp at Valley Forge (1777–78), where Baron von Steuben drilled the troops
Benedict Arnold plotted to hand West Point to the British (1780); Major John André was caught and executed as a spy
Thomas Paine’s _Common Sense_ (1776) and _The American Crisis_ (“These are the times that try men’s souls”)
The Marquis de Lafayette, a young French noble, served as a general under Washington
Henry Knox hauled cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Dorchester Heights, and the British left Boston (March 1776)
Deborah Sampson fought disguised as “Robert Shurtleff”; Mary Ludwig Hays may have inspired the “Molly Pitcher” legend at Monmouth
Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation (1775) promised freedom to enslaved people of Patriots who joined the British; many Black Loyalists later settled in Nova Scotia
Spain joined in 1779; Bernardo de Gálvez took Baton Rouge, Mobile, and Pensacola (1781)
George III refused the Olive Branch Petition (1775), written by John Dickinson, and declared the colonies in rebellion
John Paul Jones (_Bonhomme Richard_ vs. _Serapis_, 1779) is said to have shouted “I have not yet begun to fight!”
In the South: Francis Marion (the “Swamp Fox”), Daniel Morgan’s win over Banastre Tarleton at Cowpens, and Nathanael Greene
George Rogers Clark captured Fort Sackville at Vincennes (1779), in the West
Mohawk leader Joseph Brant sided with Britain; the Oneida mostly helped the Americans; the Sullivan Expedition struck the Iroquois (1779)
General Charles Lee was court-martialed for retreating at Monmouth (1778)
From Poland: Casimir Pulaski (“father of the American cavalry”) died after the Siege of Savannah; Thaddeus Kościuszko designed West Point’s fortifications
Henry Laurens, once held in the Tower of London, joined the peace talks; the treaty set the western border at the Mississippi River

trap.title: War or battle? Which war?
trap.body: This war’s battles are separate answer lines: Lexington and Concord, Bunker Hill, Trenton, Saratoga, and Yorktown, so a question asking for “this battle” wants the battle, not the war. It is also easy to mix up with the French and Indian War (1754–1763), when George Washington fought for Britain, and the War of 1812, the second U.S. war against Britain.
trap.fix: Listen for “this war” versus “this battle.” Clues about 1775–1783, the Continental Army, Valley Forge, Saratoga, Yorktown, and the 1783 Treaty of Paris mean this war. Fort Necessity, Braddock, and Quebec in 1759 mean the French and Indian War; impressment and the burning of Washington mean the War of 1812.
trap.line: Real answer line: American Revolutionary War (or Revolutionary War; accept American War of Independence; prompt on Revolution or War of Independence)

topics.name: Apollo Program
topics.kicker: NASA’s Moon-landing program, 1961–1972 · Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon
topics.briefing: In 1961, President John F. Kennedy challenged the United States to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out, and NASA’s Apollo program met that goal on July 20, 1969, when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the lunar surface. Giant Saturn V rockets sent nine crews to the Moon between 1968 and 1972; six of them landed, and twelve astronauts walked on it. Apollo 13 never landed, but its crew survived an explosion and made it home safely.
topics.answerHtml: Apollo program (or Project Apollo; accept Apollo missions; prompt on Apollo alone or on a specific mission such as Apollo 11)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: NASA official Abe Silverstein named this program in 1960 after a Greek god whom he pictured riding a chariot across the sun. This program’s Moon missions were launched by the Saturn V, the tallest rocket of its time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program that landed astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

tossups.p: Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died when a fire broke out inside their spacecraft during a launch-pad test in January 1967, early in this program. Afterward, NASA redesigned the spacecraft so that its hatch could be opened quickly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this program whose astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon.

tossups.p: On Christmas Eve 1968, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell, and Bill Anders read from the Book of Genesis while orbiting the Moon on a mission of this program, the first crewed flight to travel around the Moon.
tossups.r: Anders took the photo _Earthrise_ on that flight. For 10 points, name this NASA program that later landed astronauts on the Moon.

tossups.p: During a dress rehearsal for a Moon landing in May 1969, two astronauts in this program flew a lunar module nicknamed _Snoopy_ to within about nine miles of the Moon’s surface while the command module, _Charlie Brown_, waited above.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program whose next mission landed the first people on the Moon two months later.

tossups.p: Margaret Hamilton led a team at MIT that wrote the onboard flight software for this program’s spacecraft. During one landing, that software kept working through a series of “1202” computer alarms.
tossups.r: That landing was Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin’s in 1969. For 10 points, name this NASA program that put astronauts on the Moon.

tossups.p: After an oxygen tank exploded, the crew of one mission in this program used their lunar module, _Aquarius_, as a lifeboat, and they used tape, plastic bags, and cardboard to make square air filters fit a round opening.
tossups.r: Jack Swigert had reported, “Houston, we’ve had a problem.” For 10 points, name this NASA program whose 13th mission returned safely without landing on the Moon.

tossups.p: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during this program, and his crewmate Stuart Roosa carried tree seeds into lunar orbit that were later planted across the United States as “Moon trees.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program of the Space Race, in which twelve astronauts walked on the Moon.

tossups.p: On the first mission of this program to bring a Lunar Roving Vehicle, David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment to show that, without air, they would hit the ground together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program whose missions included the first crewed Moon landing in 1969.

tossups.p: Geologist Harrison Schmitt became the only professional scientist to walk on the Moon during this program’s final mission, whose crew also took the famous photo of the whole Earth called _The Blue Marble_.
tossups.r: His crewmate Gene Cernan was the last astronaut of this program to leave the Moon, in December 1972. For 10 points, name this NASA program.

tossups.p: At Rice University in 1962, a president declared, “We choose to go to the Moon in this decade… not because they are easy, but because they are hard.” In a 1963 speech to the United Nations, that president even suggested a joint Moon mission with the Soviet Union.
tossups.r: That president was John F. Kennedy, who had set the goal of a Moon landing “before this decade is out.” For 10 points, name this NASA program.

tossups.p: Wernher von Braun’s team at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, designed the three-stage rocket that launched this program’s Moon missions, whose first stage alone had five F-1 engines. That rocket stood about 363 feet tall.
tossups.r: That rocket was the Saturn V. For 10 points, name this NASA program that sent astronauts to the Moon.

tossups.p: John Houbolt argued that this program should use lunar orbit rendezvous, in which a small lander would leave the main spacecraft in orbit around the Moon and later rejoin it. The company Grumman built that lander.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program, which followed Projects Mercury and Gemini and first landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969.

tossups.p: The aircraft carrier USS _Hornet_ picked up one crew of this program after splashdown, and President Richard Nixon greeted the astronauts aboard the ship. They then spent weeks in quarantine in case they had carried germs back from the Moon.
tossups.r: That crew was Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. For 10 points, name this NASA program.

tossups.p: Lightning struck the rocket twice just after the launch of this program’s second Moon-landing mission, whose crew then landed near the robotic probe Surveyor 3 and brought parts of it back to Earth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program whose first landing, in July 1969, put Neil Armstrong on the Moon.

tossups.p: Scientists bounce lasers off mirrors that astronauts of this program left on the Moon in order to measure the distance between Earth and the Moon. Katherine Johnson helped calculate the flight path for this program’s first landing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NASA program in which Neil Armstrong said, “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”

First landing: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon on July 20, 1969

Armstrong: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind”
The American side of the Space Race with the Soviet Union
Its Moon missions launched on the Saturn V rocket, designed by Wernher von Braun’s team
Mission 13 (1970): an oxygen tank exploded (“Houston, we’ve had a problem”), and the crew returned safely

Mission 8 (December 1968) was the first crewed flight around the Moon; Bill Anders took _Earthrise_
The lunar module _Eagle_ landed at the Sea of Tranquility; Michael Collins orbited in the command module _Columbia_
Mission 17 (December 1972) was the last: Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt walked on the Moon
Followed Project Mercury and Project Gemini
Kennedy at Rice University (1962): “We choose to go to the Moon… because they are hard”; in 1963 he suggested a joint mission with the Soviets
Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon
Named in 1960 by NASA’s Abe Silverstein for a Greek god he pictured driving a chariot across the sun
Margaret Hamilton led MIT’s flight-software team; the software handled “1202” alarms during the first landing
Mission 10 was a dress rehearsal, with the lunar module _Snoopy_ and the command module _Charlie Brown_
On mission 13, the lunar module _Aquarius_ served as a lifeboat; the crew made square air filters fit a round opening
Alan Shepard hit golf balls on mission 14; Stuart Roosa carried seeds that became “Moon trees”
Mission 15 first used the Lunar Roving Vehicle; David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together
The final crew took the photo _The Blue Marble_; Harrison Schmitt was the only scientist to walk on the Moon
John Houbolt pushed for lunar orbit rendezvous; Grumman built the lunar module
The Saturn V was designed at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama; its first stage had five F-1 engines
The USS _Hornet_ picked up the first landing crew; Richard Nixon greeted them; they spent weeks in quarantine
Lightning struck mission 12 at launch; its crew landed near the probe Surveyor 3
Scientists bounce lasers off mirrors the astronauts left on the Moon to measure its distance
Mission 8’s astronauts read from the Book of Genesis on Christmas Eve 1968
Katherine Johnson helped calculate the flight path for the first landing

trap.title: Program, mission, or god?
trap.body: Saying just “Apollo” is risky: this answer line wants the whole program, and Apollo is also a Greek god with his own answer line. Some tossups ask for a single mission instead, such as Apollo 11 (the first landing) or Apollo 13 (the explosion). The program came after Projects Mercury and Gemini, and NASA’s later Moon program is named Artemis, after Apollo’s twin sister.
trap.fix: If the question says “this program” or “this project,” say “Apollo program.” If it says “this mission,” give the number: 8 for the first trip around the Moon, 11 for Armstrong and Aldrin, 13 for “Houston, we’ve had a problem,” and 17 for the final landing.
trap.line: Real answer line: Apollo program (or Project Apollo; accept Apollo missions; prompt on Apollo alone or on a specific mission such as Apollo 11)

topics.name: Articles of Confederation
topics.kicker: First U.S. plan of government, 1781–1789 · Replaced by the Constitution
topics.briefing: Before the Constitution, the United States ran on the Articles of Confederation, approved by Congress in 1777 and finally ratified by all thirteen states in 1781. Each state kept most of its power and had one vote in a weak Congress that could not collect taxes, regulate trade, or enforce its own laws. After indebted farmers in Massachusetts rose up in Shays’ Rebellion, leaders met in Philadelphia in 1787 to fix the Articles and ended up replacing them with the Constitution.
topics.answerHtml: Articles of Confederation (accept Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union; prompt on Articles or Confederation; do not accept “Constitution”)
accept: articles of confederation and perpetual union
the articles of confederation and perpetual union

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: One section of this document said the states were entering into “a firm league of friendship with each other” for their common defense. Another section said that each state kept its “sovereignty, freedom, and independence.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first constitution of the United States, which was replaced in 1789.

tossups.p: Under one section of this document, Canada could join the United States automatically, but any other colony needed the approval of nine states. Changing this document required the approval of all thirteen states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weak first plan of government for the United States, which took effect in 1781.

tossups.p: John Dickinson wrote the first draft of this document in 1776, and the Second Continental Congress approved a final version in York, Pennsylvania, in November 1777, after the British had captured Philadelphia.
tossups.r: This document finally went into effect in 1781. For 10 points, name this first constitution of the United States.

tossups.p: Maryland refused to approve this document until Virginia and other states gave up their claims to land in the West, which they then handed over to Congress. Because of that delay, this document did not take effect until March 1781.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan of government, written during the Revolutionary War, that the U.S. Constitution later replaced.

tossups.p: Under this document, each state had one vote in Congress no matter how many people lived there, and the most important laws needed the votes of nine of the thirteen states.
tossups.r: It created no executive branch and no national court system. For 10 points, name this first U.S. constitution, in effect from 1781 to 1789.

tossups.p: Superintendent of Finance Robert Morris struggled to pay the nation’s debts under this document, and in 1781 he helped found the Bank of North America, the first bank chartered by its Congress.
tossups.r: That Congress could not collect taxes and had to ask the states for money. For 10 points, name this first constitution of the United States.

tossups.p: General Benjamin Lincoln’s militia, paid for by Boston merchants, broke up a rebellion of indebted farmers who had tried to seize the federal arsenal at Springfield while this document was in force.
tossups.r: That uprising, led by Daniel Shays, convinced many leaders that this document was too weak. For 10 points, name this first U.S. constitution.

tossups.p: Delegates from only five states attended a 1786 meeting in Annapolis to discuss trade problems under this document, and Alexander Hamilton wrote that meeting’s call for a larger convention the next year.
tossups.r: That convention, held in Philadelphia in 1787, replaced this document with the Constitution. For 10 points, name this first plan of government for the United States.

tossups.p: At a 1785 conference held at George Washington’s home, Virginia and Maryland worked out rules for sharing the Potomac River and the Chesapeake Bay, a meeting that led to calls for fixing this document.
tossups.r: Shays’ Rebellion also exposed this document’s weaknesses. For 10 points, name this first U.S. constitution, which was replaced in 1789.

tossups.p: A law passed under this document said a territory could apply for statehood once it had 60,000 free inhabitants, and that three to five states would be carved out of its region. That same law banned slavery northwest of the Ohio River.
tossups.r: That law was the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. For 10 points, name this first constitution of the United States.

tossups.p: A 1785 law passed under this document divided western land into townships six miles on a side, each with 36 sections, and set aside one section in every township to support public schools.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first plan of national government, which lasted until the Constitution took effect in 1789.

tossups.p: In 1783, unpaid soldiers surrounded the building in Philadelphia where the Congress created by this document was meeting, so Congress moved to Princeton, New Jersey. It later met in Annapolis, Trenton, and New York.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this document whose weak central government struggled to pay its own army, the first constitution of the United States.

tossups.p: In an 1888 book, the historian John Fiske called the years from 1783 to 1789, while this document was in force, “the critical period” of American history. During those years, several states printed their own money and taxed goods from other states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first U.S. constitution, which was replaced after the Constitutional Convention of 1787.

tossups.p: Southern states were furious when John Jay, the foreign affairs secretary under this document, offered to give up American use of the Mississippi River for trade for many years in talks with Spain’s Diego de Gardoqui [“gar-DOH-kee”].
tossups.r: That deal never happened, partly because treaties under this document needed the approval of nine states. For 10 points, name this first U.S. plan of government.

tossups.p: In _Federalist_ No. 15, Alexander Hamilton complained that under this document the nation had reached “almost the last stage of national humiliation.” James Madison listed its faults in a 1787 essay called “Vices of the Political System of the United States.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first U.S. constitution, ratified in 1781 and replaced in 1789.

clues.t: The first constitution (plan of government) of the United States
Adopted by Congress in 1777, in effect from 1781, and replaced by the U.S. Constitution in 1789
Created a weak central government: a one-house Congress that could not collect taxes
Shays’ Rebellion (1786–1787) exposed its weaknesses
Each state had one vote in Congress, no matter its population
Major laws and treaties needed nine of the thirteen states; changes to it needed all thirteen
No executive branch and no national court system
Congress could not regulate trade; states printed their own money and taxed each other’s goods
Its biggest success: the Northwest Ordinance (1787) banned slavery in the Northwest Territory and set rules for statehood
Annapolis Convention (1786): only five states came; Hamilton’s report called for a convention in Philadelphia
The Constitutional Convention (Philadelphia, 1787) met to revise it but replaced it instead
Daniel Shays’s farmers tried to seize the Springfield arsenal (1787); Benjamin Lincoln’s militia, paid for by Boston merchants, broke up the rebellion
Called the union “a firm league of friendship”; each state kept its “sovereignty, freedom, and independence”
Canada could join automatically; any other colony needed nine states’ approval
John Dickinson wrote the first draft (1776); Congress approved it at York, Pennsylvania (November 1777)
Maryland approved it last (1781), after Virginia and other states gave up their western land claims
Land Ordinance of 1785: townships six miles square with 36 sections; one section supported public schools
Northwest Ordinance: 60,000 free inhabitants to apply for statehood; three to five new states
Mount Vernon Conference (1785): Virginia and Maryland settled Potomac River issues at Washington’s home
Pennsylvania Mutiny (1783): unpaid soldiers drove Congress from Philadelphia to Princeton
Historian John Fiske called the era “the critical period” of American history (1888)
John Jay’s failed deal with Spain’s Diego de Gardoqui over the Mississippi River (1786)
Superintendent of Finance Robert Morris struggled with the nation’s debts and helped found the Bank of North America (1781)
Hamilton in _Federalist_ No. 15: “almost the last stage of national humiliation”; Madison wrote “Vices of the Political System”

trap.title: First constitution, not the second
trap.body: Questions about this document often mention the Constitution, the Constitutional Convention, the Northwest Ordinance, or Shays’ Rebellion, which are all separate answer lines. The Articles were the first plan of government (1781–1789); the U.S. Constitution replaced them in 1789. Don’t confuse the Confederation (the United States of the 1780s) with the Confederacy, the Southern states of the Civil War.
trap.fix: Listen for weakness clues: one vote per state, no power to tax, no executive branch, and changes that needed all thirteen states. Those mean the Articles of Confederation. Say the full name, because “Articles” alone only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Articles of Confederation (accept Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union; prompt on Articles or Confederation; do not accept “Constitution”)

topics.name: Battle of Bunker Hill
topics.kicker: Costly British win near Boston, 1775 · Famous for “the whites of their eyes”
topics.briefing: On the night of June 16, 1775, colonial militiamen secretly dug earthworks on Breed’s Hill, overlooking Boston from the Charlestown peninsula; the battle is named for nearby Bunker Hill. The next day, British troops under General William Howe charged up the hill three times. The colonists drove back the first two attacks and retreated only when their gunpowder ran low, and the British won the hill at a cost of more than 1,000 casualties.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Bunker Hill (or Battle of Breed’s Hill; prompt on Siege of Boston or Charlestown)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At dawn, the British warship HMS _Lively_ opened fire on earthworks that colonists had secretly built overnight, starting the day of this battle. Colonel William Prescott commanded the men inside that earthen fort, called a redoubt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle on the Charlestown peninsula, a costly British victory near Boston.

tossups.p: Abigail Adams and her seven-year-old son, John Quincy, watched the smoke rising from burning Charlestown during this battle from Penn’s Hill, near their home in Braintree, Massachusetts. The next day, Abigail wrote to her husband that their dear friend Dr. Joseph Warren had been killed in this battle.
tossups.r: British troops under General William Howe won this battle only after three attacks. For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle near Boston.

tossups.p: Daniel Webster gave speeches at both the 1825 cornerstone ceremony and the 1843 dedication of a granite obelisk honoring this battle. That 221-foot monument is the last stop on Boston’s Freedom Trail.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle fought on June 17, 1775, in which colonial militia twice drove back British attacks near Boston.

tossups.p: When the Marquis de Lafayette died in 1834, he was buried in Paris under soil he had taken home from the site of this battle. Nine years earlier, he had laid the cornerstone of a monument there during his farewell tour of the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1775 battle near Boston, where colonial militia drove back two British attacks before retreating.

tossups.p: Fourteen officers signed a petition praising Salem Poor, a free Black soldier, for his bravery in this battle. Another Black soldier, Peter Salem, was credited with shooting the British major John Pitcairn during this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle in which colonists defended a hill across the river from Boston.

tossups.p: Months after this battle, Paul Revere identified the remains of his friend Joseph Warren, who had been killed in it, by recognizing a false tooth that Revere had made for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle where the colonists ran low on gunpowder and retreated after three British attacks.

tossups.p: New Hampshire troops under John Stark lined a rail fence and a narrow beach along the Mystic River to stop British light infantry from getting around the colonists’ flank in this battle, and the light infantry fell back after heavy losses.
tossups.r: Colonel William Prescott commanded the colonists’ main earthwork. For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle on the Charlestown peninsula.

tossups.p: During this battle, British cannon fire from ships and from Copp’s Hill in Boston set the nearby town of Charlestown on fire, because colonial snipers had been shooting from its buildings.
tossups.r: General William Howe’s troops finally took the colonists’ earthwork on their third attack. For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle.

tossups.p: Two days before this battle, the Second Continental Congress named George Washington commander of the Continental Army, so he was not present. Artemas Ward commanded the colonial army around Boston at the time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle fought near Boston on June 17, 1775, two months after Lexington and Concord.

tossups.p: Either Israel Putnam or William Prescott is said to have given a famous order in this battle, telling the colonists to save their scarce gunpowder by holding their fire until the enemy came very close.
tossups.r: That order was “Don’t fire until you see the whites of their eyes!” For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle.

tossups.p: After this battle’s heavy losses, General Thomas Gage was called home, and the general who had led the attack replaced him as the British commander in America. Gage had sent troops into this battle after colonists fortified the heights across the river from Boston overnight.
tossups.r: That general was William Howe. For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle on the Charlestown peninsula.

tossups.p: Colonists were ordered to fortify one hill on the Charlestown peninsula but built their main earthwork on a lower hill closer to Boston instead, so most of this battle was actually fought there.
tossups.r: This battle is still named for the first hill. For 10 points, name this battle of June 17, 1775.

tossups.p: Suffolk County, Massachusetts, which includes Boston, marks a legal holiday every June 17 in honor of this battle. At the end of this battle, the colonists retreated across the narrow Charlestown Neck to the mainland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle near Boston that came two months after the fighting at Lexington and Concord.

tossups.p: John Trumbull painted _The Death of General Warren_ at this battle, showing a Patriot leader who had recently been named a general but chose to fight as a volunteer. Warren had sent Paul Revere on his famous ride two months earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1775 battle near Boston, where William Prescott commanded the colonists’ earthwork.

tossups.p: Historians often call the British win in this battle a Pyrrhic [“PIR-ik”] victory, because more than 1,000 British soldiers were killed or wounded while capturing a single hill. The colonists, who lost far fewer men, retreated only when they ran low on gunpowder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of June 17, 1775, on the Charlestown peninsula across from Boston.

Most of the fighting took place on a lower hill closer to Boston, not on the hill the battle is named for

Abigail Adams and seven-year-old John Quincy Adams watched the smoke from Penn’s Hill in Braintree
Daniel Webster spoke at the monument’s cornerstone ceremony (1825) and its dedication (1843)

trap.title: Bunker or Breed’s?
trap.body: This battle is named for Bunker Hill, but most of the fighting happened on Breed’s Hill, a lower hill closer to Boston, so this answer line accepts either name. Players also mix it up with Lexington and Concord (April 1775, the war’s first shots) and with Dorchester Heights (March 1776), where Henry Knox’s cannons forced the British out of Boston.
trap.fix: June 1775, Charlestown, Prescott, Howe, Joseph Warren, and “the whites of their eyes” mean this battle. Paul Revere’s ride and “the shot heard round the world” mean Lexington and Concord; cannons from Fort Ticonderoga mean Dorchester Heights.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Bunker Hill (or Battle of Breed’s Hill; prompt on Siege of Boston or Charlestown)
